computer-vision: A 3x3 convolution with stride 1 and no padding is applied to a 32x32x3 image. What is the output spatial size?
Output size is (32 - 3) / 1 + 1 = 30. Without padding, each 3x3 kernel loses one pixel on every border.
A 3x3 convolution with stride 1 and padding 1 is applied to a 224x224 feature map. What is the output spatial size?
(224 + 2*1 - 3) / 1 + 1 = 224. Padding of 1 with a 3x3 kernel is the classic 'same' setting.
How many trainable parameters, including biases, does a Conv2d layer with 64 input channels, 128 output channels and a 3x3 kernel have?
Weights are 3*3*64*128 = 73,728, plus one bias per output channel (128), giving 73,856. 73,728 forgets the biases.
What is the main purpose of the skip (residual) connections in ResNet?
Letting gradients flow through identity paths so very deep nets train well
Sharing weights between layers so the model has fewer parameters
Replacing pooling layers so feature maps keep their full spatial resolution
Forcing activations to be sparse so the network generalizes better
Residual blocks learn F(x) + x, so the identity path eases optimization and reduces degradation in very deep networks.
Inception and ResNet bottleneck blocks use 1x1 convolutions mainly to do what?
Change the number of channels cheaply before costly convolutions
Increase the spatial resolution of the incoming feature map
Detect fine edges more precisely than a 3x3 kernel can
Normalize activations in place of separate batch normalization layers
A 1x1 convolution mixes channels at each pixel, so it is used to reduce (or expand) channel depth and cut computation.
Two 3x3 convolutions with stride 1 are stacked with no pooling between them. What is the receptive field of one output pixel on the input?
Each 3x3 layer adds 2 pixels to the receptive field: 3 + 2 = 5. This is why VGG replaced large kernels with stacks of 3x3 ones.
What is the key difference between YOLO and two-stage detectors such as Faster R-CNN?
YOLO predicts boxes and classes in one pass with no proposal stage
YOLO first proposes regions and then classifies each one separately
YOLO only works on grayscale images resized to a fixed square size
YOLO needs pixel-level masks as labels instead of bounding boxes
YOLO is a one-stage detector: a single network pass outputs boxes and class scores. Faster R-CNN uses a region proposal network first.
Two boxes each have an area of 100 pixels and overlap on 50 pixels. What is their Intersection over Union (IoU)?
IoU = intersection / union = 50 / (100 + 100 - 50) = 50 / 150, which is about 0.33.
A detector outputs five heavily overlapping boxes around the same car. Which post-processing step keeps only the best one?
Non-maximum suppression
Anchor box clustering
Data augmentation
Feature pyramid fusion
NMS keeps the highest-confidence box and removes others whose IoU with it exceeds a threshold.
In object detection benchmarks, what does mAP@0.5 mean?
Mean average precision, counting a hit when IoU with ground truth is 0.5 or more
Mean accuracy of class labels on images resized to half resolution
Average precision computed only over the 50 percent most confident predicted boxes
Mean anchor precision when the confidence threshold is fixed at 0.5
mAP@0.5 averages per-class AP, where a predicted box is a true positive if its IoU with a matching ground-truth box is at least 0.5.
You must count individual cells in a microscope image, each with its own mask, even when cells touch. Which task fits?
Instance segmentation
Semantic segmentation
Image classification
Depth estimation
Instance segmentation gives a separate mask per object. Semantic segmentation labels pixels by class only, so touching cells merge.
Mask R-CNN extends Faster R-CNN mainly by adding what?
A branch that predicts a binary mask for each detected region
A recurrent layer that tracks objects across video frames
A second backbone that runs on a depth map of the image
A text encoder that turns class names into prompt embeddings
Mask R-CNN adds a small fully convolutional mask head in parallel with the box and class heads.
Which Mask R-CNN component replaced RoIPool to avoid misalignment caused by rounding region coordinates?
RoIAlign with bilinear interpolation
Max pooling with a larger stride
Anchor-free center sampling
Deformable convolution kernels
RoIPool quantizes coordinates, which shifts features. RoIAlign samples at exact positions with bilinear interpolation, improving mask accuracy.
What does the Segment Anything Model (SAM) take as input to specify which object to segment?
Prompts such as clicked points, boxes or rough masks
A fixed list of the 80 COCO class identifiers
A depth map captured together with the image
Class logits produced by a separate classifier
SAM is a promptable segmentation model: an image encoder plus a prompt encoder for points, boxes or masks, and it returns masks without class labels.
You have only 500 labeled images for a new classification task. Which approach usually works best?
Freeze a pretrained backbone and train a new classification head
Train a ResNet-152 from random weights on the 500 images
Train only the first convolution layer and drop the remaining layers
Skip normalization of the images to keep their raw pixel statistics
Pretrained features transfer well, so with little data you reuse them and fit only a small head. Training a large model from scratch overfits.
In PyTorch, which loop freezes every parameter of a pretrained backbone?
for p in model.parameters(): p.requires_grad = False
for p in model.parameters(): p.grad = torch.zeros_like(p)
for p in model.parameters(): p.data.zero_()
for p in model.parameters(): p.detach()
Setting requires_grad to False stops gradient computation for those weights. p.detach() returns a new tensor and does not change p.
Which classic hand-crafted method detects keypoints and builds descriptors that are invariant to scale and rotation?
SIFT
Sobel
Canny
HOG

SIFT finds keypoints in scale space and builds orientation-normalized gradient histograms. Sobel and Canny only find edges, and HOG computes dense gradient histograms that are not scale or rotation invariant.
A ViT with 16x16 patches processes a 224x224 image. How many patch tokens are created, not counting the [CLS] token?
224 / 16 = 14 patches per side, so 14 * 14 = 196 patch tokens. With the [CLS] token the sequence length is 197.
In the original Vision Transformer, what is the [CLS] token used for?
Its final embedding is fed to the classification head
It marks where padding patches begin in the sequence
It stores the positional encoding of the top-left patch
It holds the average pixel value of the whole image
A learnable [CLS] token is prepended to the patch tokens; after the encoder, its output representation is used for classification.
Why did the original ViT need very large pretraining datasets to beat CNNs?
It has weaker built-in priors such as locality and translation equivariance
It cannot use GPUs efficiently because attention is computed sequentially
It only accepts grayscale images, so it needs more samples to learn color
It uses no positional information, so word order must be learned from scratch
Convolutions hard-code locality; ViT must learn such structure from data, so it shines with large pretraining or strong augmentation.
nlp: How does Byte Pair Encoding (BPE) build its vocabulary during training?
It repeatedly merges the most frequent adjacent pair of symbols
It keeps only whole words that appear more than a set number of times
It splits every word into fixed three-character chunks
It clusters word embeddings and assigns one token per cluster
BPE starts from characters (or bytes) and greedily merges the most frequent adjacent pair until the target vocabulary size is reached.
In BERT's WordPiece tokenizer, how are subword pieces that continue a word marked?
With a ## prefix, as in play and ##ing
With a leading underscore, as in _play
With a trailing @@ marker, as in play@@
With angle brackets, as in <ing>
WordPiece in BERT prefixes non-initial pieces with ##. The leading-space marker (a special underscore-like symbol) is used by SentencePiece.
What is the main reason modern NLP models use subword tokenization instead of whole-word vocabularies?
Rare and unseen words can be built from known pieces
It removes the need for any embedding layer
It guarantees exactly one token for every word in the text
It makes sentences shorter than with word tokens
Subwords keep the vocabulary fixed while still representing rare or new words as sequences of known units, avoiding unknown tokens.
GPT-2 uses byte-level BPE. What practical benefit does this give?
Any input string can be encoded without an unknown token
Every English word becomes exactly one token
The vocabulary needs only 256 entries in total
Tokenization no longer depends on the training corpus or its merges
Starting from the 256 possible bytes means every string is representable, so no [UNK] token is needed. Merges still build a larger vocabulary.
What limitation of early RNN encoder-decoder models did the attention mechanism of Bahdanau et al. address?
Squeezing the whole input into one fixed-length context vector
Being unable to process input sentences in more than one language
Needing labeled part-of-speech tags for every input token
Producing outputs only as long as the input sequence
Attention lets the decoder look at all encoder states at each step, instead of relying on a single vector that bottlenecks long inputs.
When training a sequence-to-sequence decoder, what is teacher forcing?
Feeding the ground-truth previous token as the next decoder input
Freezing the encoder while only the decoder is trained
Using a larger model's outputs as soft training labels
Forcing the decoder to stop exactly at the reference output length
With teacher forcing the decoder sees the correct previous token instead of its own prediction, which speeds up and stabilizes training.
Which of these models uses a full encoder-decoder Transformer architecture?
T5
BERT
GPT-2
RoBERTa
T5 frames every task as text-to-text with an encoder and a decoder. BERT and RoBERTa are encoder-only; GPT-2 is decoder-only.
A unigram bag-of-words sentiment model labels 'not good at all' as positive. Which change most directly helps?
Adding bigram features so 'not good' becomes its own feature
Lowercasing all text before the bag-of-words features are extracted
Stemming words so that 'good' and 'goods' are merged
Removing all stopwords from the input before training
Unigrams ignore word order, so negation is lost. Bigrams capture 'not good'. Removing stopwords would often drop 'not' and make it worse.
Why can removing stopwords with a standard list hurt a sentiment classifier?
Common lists include negations such as 'not' and 'no'
Stopword removal also converts all of the text to lowercase
It removes every adjective from each sentence
It splits each word into individual characters
Negation words often appear in stopword lists, yet they flip sentiment, so dropping them loses key information.
Your sentiment dataset is 90% positive. A model that always predicts 'positive' gets 90% accuracy. Which metric better reveals the problem?
Macro-averaged F1 score
Training loss curve
Overall accuracy
Number of training epochs
Macro F1 averages F1 per class, so failing on the minority class pulls the score down sharply, unlike accuracy.
Using BIO tagging for named entities, how is 'New York City' tagged as a location?
B-LOC I-LOC I-LOC
B-LOC B-LOC B-LOC
I-LOC I-LOC I-LOC
B-LOC I-LOC O
B marks the beginning of an entity, I marks tokens inside it, and O marks tokens outside any entity.
In Hugging Face token classification, what does assigning the label -100 to a token do?
The loss function ignores that token
The token is tagged as an entity
The token is dropped from the input
The token gets the highest weight
PyTorch CrossEntropyLoss uses ignore_index=-100 by default, so special tokens or extra subword pieces with that label do not affect training.
In spaCy, after doc = nlp(text), which attribute holds the detected named entities?
doc.ents
doc.entities
doc.ner
doc.labels
doc.ents is a tuple of Span objects, each with a label_ such as PERSON or ORG.
Converting 'How many users signed up in May?' into an executable SQL query is an example of which task?
Semantic parsing
Named entity recognition
Sentiment analysis
Coreference resolution
Semantic parsing maps natural language to a formal meaning representation, such as SQL, logical forms or API calls.
In text-to-SQL evaluation, what does execution accuracy measure?
Whether the predicted query returns the same result as the gold query
Whether the predicted query string exactly matches the gold string
How long the predicted query takes to run on the database
Whether the predicted query parses without any syntax errors
Execution accuracy runs both queries and compares results, so different but equivalent SQL is counted as correct, unlike exact match.
What is the difference between a causal language model (like GPT) and a masked language model (like BERT)?
Causal predicts the next token from the left; masked fills hidden tokens using both sides
Causal reads both sides of the text; masked reads only the left side of the text
Causal works only on characters; masked works only on whole words
Causal needs labeled data; masked needs only parallel translation corpora
Causal models factor text left to right. Masked models hide some tokens and predict them from the full surrounding context.
A language model's average cross-entropy on a test set is 2.0 nats per token. What is its perplexity?
About 7.39
About 4.00
About 2.00
About 100
Perplexity is exp(cross-entropy) when using natural log: e^2 is about 7.39. 100 would be the value for base 10.
In original BERT pretraining, what fraction of input tokens is selected for the masked-prediction objective?
BERT selects 15% of tokens; of those, 80% become [MASK], 10% a random token and 10% stay unchanged.
Why does a decoder-only Transformer apply a causal mask in self-attention?
So each position cannot attend to future tokens
So padding tokens get more attention weight
So attention runs in linear time over length
So each head attends to a different layer
The mask blocks attention to later positions, so training on next-token prediction does not leak the answer.
When sampling from a language model, what happens as you lower the softmax temperature toward 0?
Sampling approaches greedy decoding
Outputs become more random
All tokens get equal probability
The model stops after one token
Lower temperature sharpens the distribution toward the most likely token. Higher temperature flattens it and increases randomness.
speech-recognition: Which step comes last in the standard MFCC computation?
Taking the DCT of the log mel filterbank energies
Applying the mel filterbank to the power spectrum
Computing the FFT of each windowed frame
Applying a pre-emphasis filter to the signal
The usual order is framing and windowing, FFT, mel filterbank, log, then the discrete cosine transform that yields the cepstral coefficients.
Why do MFCCs use the mel scale instead of a linear frequency scale?
It mimics human pitch perception, with finer detail at low frequencies
It removes all of the background noise from the recording before analysis
It doubles the sampling rate so high frequencies are kept intact
It turns the signal into text tokens that a decoder can read
The mel scale is roughly linear below about 1 kHz and logarithmic above, matching how humans perceive pitch differences.
Speech features are computed on short overlapping frames. Which setting is a common choice?
25 ms windows with a 10 ms hop
1 s windows with a 500 ms hop
2 ms windows with a 1 ms hop
250 ms windows with a 100 ms hop
Speech is roughly stationary over 20 to 30 ms, so 25 ms windows shifted by 10 ms are a standard compromise.
What does the discrete cosine transform contribute to MFCC features?
It decorrelates filterbank energies and packs information into a few coefficients
It converts the raw waveform from the time domain into the frequency domain directly
It resamples the audio to 16 kHz before the filterbank is applied
It removes silence at the beginning and the end of the utterance
Neighboring mel bands are highly correlated; the DCT decorrelates them, and keeping about 13 coefficients captures the spectral envelope.
For mono audio, what is the shape of the array returned by librosa.feature.mfcc(y=y, sr=sr, n_mfcc=13)?
(13, number_of_frames)
(number_of_frames, 13)
(1, 13, number_of_frames)
(13, len(y) // sr)
librosa returns coefficients along the first axis and time frames along the second, so you often transpose it for frame-major models.
What problem does Connectionist Temporal Classification (CTC) loss solve in speech recognition?
Training without a frame-by-frame alignment of audio to text
Removing background noise from the audio before training begins
Translating speech directly into a different language
Splitting long recordings into sentences automatically
CTC sums over all valid alignments between input frames and the shorter label sequence, so only the transcript is needed.
A CTC model outputs the frame path h h _ e l l _ l o o, where _ is the blank symbol. What is the decoded text?
hello
helo
hhelo
hellloo
CTC decoding first merges repeated symbols (h _ e l _ l o), then removes blanks, giving hello. The blank keeps the two l's separate.
In CTC, how can a model output the word 'too', which has a double letter?
By emitting a blank between the two o frames
By emitting the o symbol twice in a row
By switching to a separate double-letter token
By lowering the frame rate of the encoder
Consecutive identical symbols are merged, so o o collapses to one o. A blank in between (o _ o) preserves both letters.
Why do CTC-based recognizers often benefit from an external language model during decoding?
CTC treats each frame's output as independent given the audio
CTC cannot produce any output sequence longer than ten characters
CTC requires a language model to compute its loss
CTC can only output phonemes, not characters
CTC makes a conditional independence assumption between output steps, so it models linguistic context weakly; an LM adds that context.
In a classic hybrid ASR system, what does the language model score?
How likely a word sequence is, independent of the audio
How well each audio frame matches a phoneme state
How loud the speaker is relative to the background noise level
How many frames each word should occupy in time
The acoustic model scores the audio given units like phonemes; the language model scores P(words), and the decoder combines both.
Your ASR system keeps transcribing rare medical terms as common sound-alike words. Which change most directly targets this?
Adapting the language model with medical text
Increasing the number of MFCC coefficients
Shortening the analysis window to 5 ms
Converting the audio from mono to stereo
The acoustic evidence is similar, so the language model decides. Domain text raises the probability of the correct terms.
In end-to-end ASR, what is shallow fusion?
Adding a weighted external LM log-probability to the model score in beam search
Training the acoustic model and the language model as one single network
Averaging the weights of two acoustic models trained on different data
Concatenating MFCC and spectrogram features at the model input layer
Shallow fusion keeps models separate and combines their scores at decoding time: log P_asr + lambda * log P_lm.
A 10-word reference is recognized with 1 substitution, 1 deletion and 1 insertion. What is the word error rate?
WER = (S + D + I) / N = (1 + 1 + 1) / 10 = 30%. The denominator is the number of reference words.
What is the core architecture of OpenAI's Whisper model?
An encoder-decoder Transformer working on log-Mel spectrograms
A CTC-only convolutional model operating on raw waveforms
A hidden Markov model with Gaussian mixture emissions per phoneme state
A decoder-only language model that reads MFCC feature tokens
Whisper encodes log-Mel spectrogram frames with a Transformer encoder and generates text tokens with a Transformer decoder.
The Whisper model processes audio in fixed segments of what length?
30 seconds
5 seconds
60 seconds
10 seconds
Whisper pads or trims input to 30-second windows; longer audio is transcribed by moving through successive windows.
How does Whisper's decoder know whether to transcribe or to translate the audio?
Special task tokens in the decoder's starting prompt
A separate model checkpoint for each of the two tasks
The sample rate chosen for the input audio file
A flag stored in the header of the spectrogram
Whisper is multitask: tokens for language, task (transcribe or translate) and timestamps are placed at the start of the decoder sequence.
Whisper's built-in 'translate' task produces text in which language?
English
Its input language
Any target language
Chinese
Whisper was trained for X to English speech translation; transcribing in the source language is the separate 'transcribe' task.
What is beam search with a beam width of 1 equivalent to?
Greedy decoding
Exhaustive search
Random sampling
CTC prefix scoring
Keeping only one hypothesis per step means always choosing the single best next token, which is greedy decoding.
What is the main trade-off when increasing the beam width in ASR decoding?
More hypotheses are explored at the cost of more computation
The model's weights are updated more often during decoding
The optimal transcript is then guaranteed to be found
Decoding becomes faster because fewer paths are scored
A wider beam reduces search errors but costs more time and memory; it is still a heuristic with no optimality guarantee.
Without length normalization, why does beam search tend to favor short hypotheses?
Each added token adds a negative log-probability to the total score
Short hypotheses tend to match the audio more closely
The beam is pruned to remove any hypothesis longer than average
The end-of-sequence token gets a large fixed bonus
Log-probabilities are negative, so longer sequences accumulate lower scores. Dividing by length (or a length penalty) corrects this bias.
multimodal-models: What training objective does CLIP use?
A contrastive loss that matches images with their paired captions
A captioning loss that generates text from images one word at a time
A pixel reconstruction loss on masked image patches
A classification loss over the 1,000 ImageNet classes
CLIP trains an image encoder and a text encoder so matching pairs have high cosine similarity and mismatched pairs in the batch have low similarity.
How does CLIP perform zero-shot image classification?
It embeds a text prompt per label and picks the most similar one
It fine-tunes a new head on a few labeled images per class
It generates a caption and searches it for a class name
It clusters image embeddings and then names each resulting cluster
Labels are turned into prompts like 'a photo of a dog', encoded, and the class whose text embedding is closest to the image embedding wins.
In a CLIP training batch of N image-text pairs, how many positive pairs does the contrastive loss use?
N
N squared
2N
The N x N similarity matrix has the N true pairs on the diagonal; the other N^2 - N entries act as negatives.
What does the learnable temperature (logit scale) do in CLIP?
Scales cosine similarities before the softmax to control its sharpness
Sets the learning rate of the text encoder relative to the image encoder
Decides how many image patches the vision encoder keeps
Controls the randomness of captions sampled at inference
Cosine similarities lie in [-1, 1]; multiplying by a learned scale lets the softmax become sharp enough for effective contrastive training.
How does LLaVA connect its vision encoder to the language model?
A learned projection maps CLIP image features into the LLM's embedding space
The LLM reads a caption written by a separate captioning model first
Image pixels are converted to ASCII characters and fed to the LLM as plain text
The vision encoder replaces the bottom layers of the language model
LLaVA projects CLIP ViT patch features (with a linear layer, later an MLP) into visual tokens placed alongside text tokens.
In a cross-attention layer where text tokens attend to image features, where do the queries come from?
The text tokens
The image features
A fixed random matrix
The output vocabulary
In cross-attention, queries come from one sequence (here text) while keys and values come from the other (image features).
A cross-attention layer has 20 text tokens as queries and 196 image patches as keys. What is the shape of one head's attention weight matrix?
Attention weights have one row per query and one column per key: 20 rows, 196 columns, each row summing to 1.
How does Flamingo inject visual information into a frozen pretrained language model?
Through gated cross-attention layers inserted between frozen LM layers
By fine-tuning every LM weight on paired image and caption data
By converting each image into a long string of text descriptions for the LM
By replacing the LM tokenizer with an image patch tokenizer
Flamingo keeps the LM frozen and adds new cross-attention blocks with tanh gates initialized at zero, so training starts from the original LM.
What is the key difference between self-attention and cross-attention?
Self-attention takes Q, K and V from one sequence; cross-attention takes K and V from another
Self-attention works only on images, while cross-attention works only on text
Self-attention has no learned weights, while cross-attention has learned weights
Self-attention runs in the encoder only, while cross-attention runs in every layer
Both use the same scaled dot-product mechanism; the difference is where keys and values come from.
What does a VQ-VAE style image tokenizer enable in unified-token multimodal models?
Images become discrete codebook tokens that one Transformer can model with text
Images are stored as raw JPEG bytes that the text tokenizer then reads directly
Text is rendered into images so the model sees only pixel inputs
Image features are averaged into one vector appended after the text
Vector quantization maps image patches to entries in a learned codebook, so images and text share one token sequence and vocabulary.
A model concatenates image patch tokens and text tokens into one sequence and processes them with the same Transformer from the first layer. What is this called?
Early fusion
Late fusion
Model ensembling
Knowledge distillation
Early fusion mixes modalities from the start. Late fusion encodes each modality separately and only combines the final outputs.
A vision encoder uses 14x14 pixel patches. If input resolution grows from 224x224 to 448x448, how does the number of visual tokens change?
It becomes 4 times larger
It becomes 2 times larger
It stays the same
It becomes 8 times larger
Tokens per side go from 16 to 32, so the total goes from 256 to 1,024, a factor of 4, which strongly affects context length and cost.
In a typical encoder-decoder image captioning model, how is the caption produced at inference time?
The decoder generates tokens one at a time conditioned on image features
The encoder outputs the whole caption in a single step as one fixed vector
A nearest neighbor search copies a caption from the training data
A classifier picks one sentence from a fixed list of templates
The image is encoded once; the text decoder then autoregressively predicts each next word, attending to the image features.
Which metric was designed for image captioning and weights n-grams by TF-IDF against multiple reference captions?
CIDEr
BLEU
Word error rate
Perplexity
CIDEr measures consensus with several human captions using TF-IDF weighted n-gram similarity. BLEU has no TF-IDF weighting.
Many classic VQA models such as those trained on VQA v2 frame answering as what kind of problem?
Classification over a fixed set of frequent answers
Regression of a single number for every question
Object detection with one box per answer word
Retrieval of the most similar training question
Most VQA v2 answers are short, so models classify over the top few thousand answers rather than generating free text.
Why did the VQA v2 dataset add complementary image pairs for the same question?
To reduce language priors that let models answer without looking at the image
To double the dataset size so that larger models could be trained
To include images from video frames as well as from still photos
To test models on questions written in several different languages
For each question there are similar images with different answers, so guessing from the question alone (for example 'yes') no longer works.
The VQA accuracy metric is commonly written as min(number of annotators who gave the answer / 3, 1). Under it, when does an answer get full credit?
When at least 3 of the 10 human annotators gave that answer
When it matches the single answer chosen by the dataset authors
When its embedding is within a set distance of the reference
When at least half of the annotators gave a similar answer
An answer given by 3 or more of the 10 annotators scores 1, so the metric tolerates disagreement. The official code also averages over annotator subsets.
You need text search over 1 million product images with low latency. Which approach fits best?
A CLIP-style dual encoder with precomputed image embeddings
Running a generative VLM on every image for every query
Captioning all images again each time a query arrives
Training a new image classifier for each search query
Dual encoders let you embed images once, index them, and compare a single text embedding per query. Generative models are far too slow for this.
Why do CLIP zero-shot pipelines wrap labels in templates like 'a photo of a {label}'?
Prompts resembling training captions usually improve accuracy
The text encoder rejects inputs shorter than five words
Templates make the image encoder run faster at inference
Without templates CLIP returns only text and no scores
CLIP was trained on full captions, so sentence-like prompts match its text distribution better than single words and often raise accuracy.
While training a captioning decoder with teacher forcing, what is the decoder input at step t?
The ground-truth caption token from step t - 1
The token the decoder predicted at step t - 1
A random token sampled from the vocabulary
The image feature vector repeated at every step
Teacher forcing feeds the correct previous token, which makes training stable and parallel; at inference the model uses its own predictions.
reinforcement-learning: What does the Markov property of an MDP state?
The next state depends only on the current state and action
The reward is the same for every state and action pair
The agent must visit every state at least once in each episode
The next state depends on the full history of past states
Under the Markov property the current state summarizes everything relevant from the past for predicting what happens next.
In the MDP tuple (S, A, P, R, gamma), which element gives the probability of the next state?
P, the transition function
R, the reward function
gamma, the discount factor
A, the action set
P(s' | s, a) defines the environment dynamics: the probability of landing in s' after taking action a in state s.
With a discount factor of 0.9 and a reward of 1 at every step forever, what is the discounted return?
Infinite
The return is a geometric series: 1 + 0.9 + 0.81 + ... = 1 / (1 - 0.9) = 10. Discounting keeps infinite-horizon returns finite.
What behavior does a discount factor of gamma = 0 produce?
The agent cares only about the immediate reward
The agent values all future rewards equally
The agent ignores the reward for the current step
The agent stops exploring after the first episode
With gamma = 0 every future reward is multiplied by zero, so the agent is fully myopic.
Q-learning update: Q(s,a) = 2, learning rate 0.5, reward 1, gamma 0.9, and max Q(s', a') = 10. What is the new Q(s,a)?
What makes Q-learning an off-policy algorithm?
Its target uses the max over next actions, not the action actually taken
It updates values only after a full episode has finished
It learns a policy network directly instead of a table of state values
It acts only with the greedy policy and does not explore
Q-learning learns about the greedy policy while acting with another (for example epsilon-greedy). SARSA uses the next action actually taken, so it is on-policy.
Why does DQN train on minibatches sampled from an experience replay buffer?
To break the correlation between consecutive transitions
To avoid needing a neural network for the Q-function
To make the environment respond faster to each action it receives
To make every reward in the batch positive
Consecutive samples are highly correlated; random replay makes updates closer to i.i.d. and reuses past experience efficiently.
How does Double DQN reduce the overestimation of Q-values?
The online network selects the next action and the target network evaluates it
It trains two agents in parallel and keeps the one with the higher total reward
It doubles the replay buffer size so that rare transitions are sampled
It averages the Q-values of all actions instead of taking the max
Using the same network to both pick and evaluate the max action biases estimates upward; decoupling the two reduces this bias.
In the REINFORCE policy gradient algorithm, what happens to actions that were followed by high returns?
Their log-probability is pushed up in proportion to the return
They are removed from the action space for all of the later episodes
Their Q-values are copied into a separate target network
Their rewards are clipped to keep the gradient small
The gradient estimate is the sum of grad log pi(a|s) times the return, so good actions become more likely.
Why do policy gradient methods subtract a baseline, such as V(s), from the return?
It reduces gradient variance without biasing the estimate
It makes every reward positive so that learning becomes more stable
It turns the method into an off-policy algorithm
It removes the need for a discount factor gamma
A baseline that does not depend on the action keeps the expected gradient unchanged while lowering its variance.
A robot arm is controlled by continuous joint torques. Why are policy gradient methods often preferred over tabular Q-learning here?
Q-learning needs a max over actions, which is hard in a continuous space
Policy gradients do not need any reward signal to learn the task
Tabular Q-learning only supports environments with fewer than ten states
Policy gradients guarantee finding the global optimum in one episode
A policy can output the parameters of a continuous distribution, such as a Gaussian, while argmax over infinitely many actions is impractical in tabular Q-learning.

It clips rewards to the range from -1 to 1 before each update
It clips the gradient norm of the value network to a fixed value
It removes episodes shorter than a fixed length from the batch

The actor simulates the environment; the critic chooses actions
The actor stores replay data; the critic samples minibatches
The actor sets the rewards; the critic sets the discount factor

Catastrophic forgetting
Policy collapse
Test set overfitting

Multiplying every reward by a random factor each step
Giving a bonus whenever the agent repeats an action

To keep the replay buffer from growing too large

A uniformly random arm on every pull, ignoring all past results

Spills objects to external storage, such as local disk

Values spread uniformly on a log scale between the bounds

A callback logger
